citation: Varghese KS, Ahmed A, Mathew DM, Fusco PJ, Abraham MN. Eutectic mixture of local anesthetics and amethocaine as topical anesthetics in pediatrics: a meta-analysis. Pediatr Res 2024;96(1):51-56.
text_quality: ok: all 6 PDF pages (journal pages 51-56), Table 1 and the six forest plots (Figs. 1-6) are in the text; PDF pages 3-5 were rendered and every study-level and pooled estimate was checked against the figures. The online supplement (search strategy, PRISMA flow, Newcastle-Ottawa scores, Supplementary Table 4 with the citations of the included studies, leave-one-out analyses) is not in the packet. The included studies other than van Kan 1997 are not in the reference list; they were identified in PubMed by author, year and topic, except 'Ormandy 1998', which PubMed does not hold under that name or topic.
design: Systematic review with pairwise meta-analysis (PRISMA and MOOSE cited; no protocol registration mentioned; search end date not given in the text). PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Cochrane Library searched from inception for RCTs and comparative cohort studies of EMLA cream versus amethocaine gel in children under 18 having any skin procedure. 10 studies included: Table 1 labels 8 as RCTs and 2 (Lawson 1995, 'Ormandy 1998') as comparative studies, yet the discussion states the analysis 'was limited to observational studies'. Study quality was rated only with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies (all studies above seven stars, called good quality); there is no Cochrane risk-of-bias assessment of the randomised trials and no GRADE or other certainty-of-evidence rating. Random-effects pooling in R (meta, metafor), Mantel-Haenszel, risk ratios (the methods text says 'risk ratios (OR)') and standardised mean differences, I2, leave-one-out sensitivity analyses (supplementary). Worker's check, not the authors': recomputing from the plotted study estimates, a random-effects model with the Hartung-Knapp adjustment reproduces every printed pooled interval and p value; ordinary DerSimonian-Laird pooling of the same estimates gives first-attempt cannulation success RR 0.98 (95% CI 0.89-1.09, p 0.72; none of the three trials significant on its own) and child-reported acceptable anaesthesia RR 0.73 (0.61-0.87; both trials favouring amethocaine on their own), so the significance of these two outcomes depends on the pooling method, while child-reported absence of pain stays significant either way (RR 0.58, 0.46-0.73). The paper calls itself 'the first and most comprehensive review on the topic' but does not cite the 2006 Cochrane review of the same comparison (Lander 2006, PMID 16856039: 6 RCTs, 534 children); it does cite Taddio 2002 (8 studies) and Pywell 2015 (3 RCTs).
population: Children under 18 having topical anaesthesia before a skin procedure (review inclusion criterion). Included studies per Table 1: age ranges from 3 months to 16 years, mean age 4.8 to 8 years, 29-51% female; procedures venous or intravenous cannulation (6 studies), venepuncture (2), Port-a-Cath puncture in children with cancer (Bishai 1999) and pulsed dye laser treatment of port-wine stain (McCafferty 1997). McCafferty 1997 is not a paediatric needle-procedure study: Table 1 gives its inclusion criterion as 'age more than 12 yr' while listing the age range as '<= 12', PubMed indexes it as adolescents and adults (no child MeSH term), the procedure is laser treatment, and EMLA, amethocaine and placebo were compared on areas of the same lesions; it feeds three of the six outcomes (Figs. 2, 3 and 6). No included study is in non-procedural (chronic or neuropathic) pain.
n: 10 studies in Table 1. Text: 892 children pooled (448 EMLA, 473 amethocaine); the two arms sum to 921, which equals the Table 1 arm totals, and within-patient designs (McCafferty 1997; Bishai 1999, a crossover) count the same patients in both arms. Studies per outcome: first-attempt cannulation success 3 (Arendts 2008, Newbury 2009, Ormandy 1998); child-reported absence of pain 5 (Arrowsmith 2000, Lawson 1995, McCafferty 1997, Ormandy 1998, Romsing 1999); child-reported VAS 4 (Bishai 1999, Choy 1999, McCafferty 1997, Newbury 2009); parent-reported VAS 2 (Bishai 1999, Choy 1999); observed pain score 3 contributing (Choy 1999, Lawson 1995, Romsing 1999; Ormandy 1998 listed without an estimate); child-reported acceptable anaesthesia 2 (Lawson 1995, McCafferty 1997). Van Kan 1997 (32 EMLA, 34 tetracaine; the one included trial reporting EMLA as more efficacious) contributes to none of the six analyses. Newbury 2009 is entered as 32 and 33 children (its observed-pain subset of 65), and its plotted first-attempt interval fits about 32 children per arm, although the trial analysed first-attempt success in 679 children.
setting: Review by authors at CUNY School of Medicine and the Feinstein Institutes, New York. Included studies 1995-2009 from Wales, Ireland, Canada, New Zealand, Australia, England, Denmark, the Netherlands and Scotland (2); settings emergency department (2), clinic or day-case unit, operating room, paediatric ward, day-case surgical unit, not stated (4).
intervention: EMLA cream (eutectic lidocaine-prilocaine, product strength [dose figure omitted]) applied to intact skin before the procedure, for the longer application time EMLA needs.
comparator: Amethocaine (tetracaine) gel, product strength [dose figure omitted], applied for a shorter time; no placebo arm in the pooled comparisons (McCafferty 1997 also had a placebo area, not used).
route: Topical, on intact skin under occlusion, before needle procedures (venous or intravenous cannulation, venepuncture, Port-a-Cath puncture) or, in one study, pulsed dye laser treatment.
duration: One application before one procedure in each study; no repeated or chronic use, no follow-up beyond the procedure.
outcomes: Six pooled outcomes, EMLA versus amethocaine, random effects, as printed: first-attempt cannulation success RR 0.98 (95% CI 0.97-0.99), p = 0.017, I2 0%, 3 studies; child-reported absence of pain RR 0.58 (0.41-0.82), p = 0.011, I2 20.2%, 5 studies; child-reported VAS SMD 0.43 (-1.46 to 2.31), p = 0.525, I2 92.8%, 4 studies; parent-reported VAS SMD -0.05 (-0.64 to 0.54), p = 0.478, I2 0%, 2 studies; observed pain score SMD -0.45 (-2.27 to 1.38), p = 0.405, I2 88.6%, 3 studies; child-reported acceptable anaesthesia RR 0.73 (0.34-1.55), p = 0.118, I2 0%, 2 studies. Study-level estimates from the forest plots: Fig. 1 Arendts 2008 RR 0.98 [0.82; 1.17], Newbury 2009 0.99 [0.75; 1.31], Ormandy 1998 0.98 [0.85; 1.13]; Fig. 2 Arrowsmith 2000 0.62 [0.41; 0.96], Lawson 1995 0.50 [0.32; 0.78], McCafferty 1997 0.33 [0.12; 0.91], Ormandy 1998 0.67 [0.54; 0.85], Romsing 1999 0.22 [0.06; 0.86]; Fig. 3 Bishai 1999 SMD -0.34 [-0.97; 0.30], Choy 1999 0.25 [-0.43; 0.92], McCafferty 1997 2.17 [1.51; 2.82], Newbury 2009 -0.35 [-0.84; 0.14]; Fig. 4 Bishai 1999 -0.09 [-0.72; 0.53], Choy 1999 0.00 [-0.67; 0.67]; Fig. 5 Choy 1999 0.00 [-0.67; 0.67], Lawson 1995 -1.26 [-1.67; -0.85], Romsing 1999 0.00 [-0.54; 0.54]; Fig. 6 Lawson 1995 RR 0.77 [0.61; 0.96], McCafferty 1997 0.68 [0.52; 0.89]. Direction labels are inconsistent: Fig. 2 places risk ratios below 1 under 'Favors amethocaine', while Fig. 6 places its two risk ratios below 1 (fewer children with acceptable anaesthesia on EMLA) under 'Favors EMLA'. Not pooled: adverse effects, erythema or blanching, time to cannulation, onset, depth or duration of anaesthesia (some were extracted to Supplementary Table 2 only).

key_results.quote: After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 10 studies were included in the final meta-analysis (Table 1, Supplementary Table 4). At quality assessment, all reports received higher than seven asterisks, indicating good quality.

A total of 892 pediatric patients were pooled, of whom 448 underwent topical anesthesia with EMLA cream and 473 underwent topical anesthesia with amethocaine gel. The number of patients in each study ranged from 17 to 109, while the mean age ranged from 4.8 to 8 years old.

Compared to amethocaine gel, EMLA cream was associated with lower rates of first cannulation success (RR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.97–0.99; p = 0.017). No heterogeneity was seen between the studies (I2 = 0%) (Fig. 1).

Compared to amethocaine gel, EMLA cream was associated with lower rates of child-reported absence of pain (RR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.41–0.82; p = 0.011). Heterogeneity between the studies was low (I2 = 20.2%) (Fig. 2).

There were no significant differences between EMLA cream and amethocaine gel for child-reported VAS (SMD, 0.43; 95% CI, −1.46 to 2.31; p = 0.525). There was high heterogeneity between the studies (I2 = 92.8%) (Fig. 3).

There were no significant differences between EMLA cream and amethocaine gel for parent-reported VAS (SMD, −0.05; 95% CI, −0.64 to 0.54; p = 0.478). No heterogeneity was seen between the studies (I2 = 0%) (Fig. 4).

There were no significant differences between EMLA cream and amethocaine gel for observed pain score (SMD, −0.45; 95% CI, −2.27 to 1.38; p = 0.405). I2 was 88.6%, indicating high heterogeneity between the studies (Fig. 5).

There were no significant differences seen between EMLA cream and amethocaine gel for child-reported acceptable anesthesia (RR, … 0.73; 95% CI, 0.34 to 1.55; p = 0.118). No heterogeneity was seen between the studies (I2 = 0%) (Fig. 6).

Presently, this pairwise meta-analysis of 10 studies pooling over 890 pediatric patients undergoing topical anesthesia with EMLA cream or amethocaine gel is the first and most comprehensive review on the topic.

Amethocaine gel is superior to EMLA cream for child-reported absence of pain and first cannulation success. There were no differences seen between EMLA cream and amethocaine gel for child-reported acceptable anesthesia or observed pain score.

The PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane Library libraries were comprehensively searched without restriction from inception to identify randomized control trials (RCTs) and comparative cohort studies comparing EMLA cream and amethocaine gel in pediatric patients undergoing topical anesthesia.
evaluated the quality of each study using the Newcastle Ottawa Scale
McCafferty/1997 … Inclusion criteria: age more than 12 yr of age, a portwine stain
Similarly, in a 2017 meta-analysis of 3 RCTs, Pywell et al. issued a weak recommendation for the use of amethocaine in the pediatric cannulation when compared with EMLA.

Taddio et al. performed a systematic review in 2001 composed of 8 studies comparing lidocaine–prilocaine with tetracaine in children for 4 different procedures: intravenous cannulation, venipuncture, Port-a-Cath puncture, and laser therapy.

Lidocaine-prilocaine and tetracaine appeared to be equally effective for procedural pain relief when used according to instructions. Tetracaine, however, is more effective when applied for the same period of time as lidocaine-prilocaine.

author_limitations.quote: This pairwise meta-analysis must be interpreted in the context of its limitations with respect to pain assessment. The reliance on child-reported, visual analogue, and observational pain scores, devoid of a universally accepted rating scale, introduced a limitation in the precision and comparability of the collected data.
Furthermore, many of the trials employed measurement tools that were not adequately established or evaluated through psychometric testing.
Additionally, variable application methods and durations of the two topical anesthetics, amethocaine gel [dose figure omitted] and EMLA cream [dose figure omitted], posed a limitation to this study.
This lack of standardization in application duration introduces a potential confounding factor that requires consideration when interpreting the results of this study
Due to differences in cream amounts and application durations, a double-blinded comparison could not be performed among the included trials.
First, due to a lack of randomized trials comparing amethocaine gel and EMLA cream, this analysis was limited to observational studies and any subsequent confounder or treatment allocation bias.

Second, this pooled analysis included data from multiple centers, each presenting unique operator experiences with topical anesthesia in pediatric populations and learning curves that may have influenced outcomes.
Of note, there is a high degree of heterogeneity between the two groups.

In pediatric patients undergoing topical anesthesia during a wide array of skin-related procedures, there is a scarcity of randomized control trials assessing the efficacy of EMLA cream and amethocaine gel.
These findings support the use of amethocaine gel in pediatric patients, although large, randomized trials comparing EMLA cream and amethocaine gel in pediatric patients are still needed.

funding_conflicts: No funding statement in the text. 'The authors declare no competing interests.' (PDF page 6). Patient consent not required (review of published studies). Two authors contributed equally; correspondence Kathryn S. Varghese, CUNY School of Medicine.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Included trial (Table 1; Fig. 2). Single-blind randomised study in 120 children, venous cannulation, EMLA vs amethocaine gel; amethocaine gave lower pain scores. Bears on D068 and on any statement comparing the two creams in children.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: McCafferty DF, Woolfson AD, Handley J, Allen G. Effect of percutaneous local anaesthetics on pain reduction during pulse dye laser treatment of portwine stains. Br J Anaesth 1997;78:286-9.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Included (Figs. 2, 3, 6) although not a paediatric needle-procedure study: Table 1 inclusion criterion 'age more than 12 yr', PubMed MeSH adolescents and adults, pulsed dye laser on facial port-wine stains, EMLA vs amethocaine vs placebo on areas of the same lesions, 29 patients; amethocaine better than EMLA. Carries the largest effect in Fig. 3.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Bishai R, Taddio A, Bar-Oz B, Freedman MH, Koren G. Relative efficacy of amethocaine gel and lidocaine-prilocaine cream for Port-a-Cath puncture in children. Pediatrics 1999;104:e31.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Included (Figs. 3, 4). Randomised blinded crossover in 39 children aged 5-16 with cancer, Port-a-Cath puncture; no difference in pain, amethocaine applied for half the time.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Newbury C, Herd DW. Amethocaine versus EMLA for successful intravenous cannulation in a children's emergency department: a randomised controlled study. Emerg Med J 2009;26:487-91.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Included (Figs. 1, 3). Parallel double-blind RCT, children 3 months-15 years, ED; first-attempt success analysed in 679 children (75.8% vs 73.9%, no difference), pain observed in 65. Varghese enters it as 32 + 33 children. Bears on cannulation-success statements.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Arendts G, Stevens M, Fry M. Topical anaesthesia and intravenous cannulation success in paediatric patients: a randomized double-blind trial. Br J Anaesth 2008;100:521-4.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Included (Fig. 1). Double-blind RCT, 177 children aged 12 months-12 years analysed, ED; first-attempt success 75% amethocaine vs 74% EMLA, no difference.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Choy L, Collier J, Watson AR. Comparison of lignocaine-prilocaine cream and amethocaine gel for local analgesia before venepuncture in children. Acta Paediatr 1999;88:961-4.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Included (Figs. 3, 4, 5). Single-blind RCT, 34 children aged 1-14, venepuncture; no difference between the creams.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Romsing J, Henneberg SW, Walther-Larsen S, Kjeldsen C. Tetracaine gel vs EMLA cream for percutaneous anaesthesia in children. Br J Anaesth 1999;82:637-8.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Included (Figs. 2, 5). Double-blind RCT, 60 children aged 3-15, venous cannulation; lower pain with tetracaine, and a third group cannulated hours after tetracaine removal (duration of topical anaesthesia).

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: van Kan HJ, Egberts AC, Rijnvos WP, ter Pelkwijk NJ, Lenderink AW. Tetracaine versus lidocaine-prilocaine for preventing venipuncture-induced pain in children. Am J Health Syst Pharm 1997;54:388-92.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Listed in Table 1 (ref 15) but in none of the six pooled analyses. Open randomised trial, 66 inpatients aged 1-15, venipuncture; EMLA judged more efficacious (97% vs 76% adequate relief, phlebotomist-rated); tetracaine and its metabolite measured in serum; erythema with tetracaine, blanching with EMLA.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Lawson RA, Smart NG, Gudgeon AC, Morton NS. Evaluation of an amethocaine gel preparation for percutaneous analgesia before venous cannulation in children. Br J Anaesth 1995;75:282-5.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Included (Figs. 2, 5, 6); labelled 'comparative study' by Varghese, indexed as RCT. Open study of amethocaine in 148 children, then single-blind comparison with EMLA in 94 patients with the same application time for both (shorter than EMLA's labelled minimum); clinically acceptable conditions 85% vs 66%. Varghese lists 55 + 55.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: 'Ormandy 1998' (Scotland, day-case surgical unit; 103 EMLA vs 109 amethocaine; children over one year before intravenous induction; labelled comparative study). Full citation only in the online Supplementary Table 4.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Included (Figs. 1, 2, 5) and the largest study; not found in PubMed by author name or by topic (1997-1999 searches, 125-record EMLA-vs-amethocaine set), so its design and population could not be checked.
